Newly hatched individuals of the African giant snail, Achatina achatina, exhibit a shell length of approximately 0.6 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.6 centimeters] at the moment of emergence from the egg. This remarkably small size, roughly equivalent to the width of a garden pea, belies the substantial growth potential the species will demonstrate over its life. Neonates are fully formed miniature versions of the adults, possessing a delicate, translucent shell that will rapidly calcify and darken as they begin exogenous feeding. Under optimal laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the incubation period from oviposition to hatching is relatively brief, with emergence occurring after approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. This short embryonic phase is typical for large terrestrial gastropods adapted to warm, humid tropical environments, where rapid development reduces vulnerability to desiccation and predation in the egg stage. The timing of hatching represents a critical energetic bottleneck, as the hatchling must immediately locate a suitable food source to sustain its transition from reliance on yolk reserves to active grazing on decaying plant matter and fungi.

The maximum lifespan of Achatina achatina under controlled captive conditions has been documented to span approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when individuals are maintained at a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This longevity is substantial for a terrestrial gastropod, placing it among the longer-lived members of the Achatinidae family. In comparison to smaller-bodied congeneric species, which often complete their life cycles in three to five years, the Achatina achatina appears to invest in a slower pace of life, featuring a protracted somatic growth phase and delayed reproductive onset. The extended lifespan reflects a physiological strategy that prioritizes gradual, continuous shell accretion over rapid attainment of terminal size. Field records from natural populations in West Africa, where thermal and humidity fluctuations are more pronounced, suggest that senescence-related mortality typically occurs somewhat earlier, although captive records provide the most reliable estimate of the species' physiological potential. This decadelong lifespan is concurrent with a gradual decline in locomotor activity and feeding efficiency during the final two to three years, consistent with age-related deterioration of the columellar muscle and sensory tentacles.

Reproductive maturity in Achatina achatina occurs at a notably advanced age relative to other large snails, with puberty being attained at roughly 335.5 days since birth [tp = roughly 335.5 days since birth] under culture conditions kept steadily at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period is over eleven months in duration, a delay that reflects the substantial energetic investment required for the individual to accumulate sufficient calcium carbonate reserves for shell thickening and to develop the complex reproductive tract characteristic of hermaphroditic stylommatophorans. Reaching this developmental milestone marks the initiation of gametogenesis and the onset of copulatory behavior, after which the snail can function reproductively as both a male and a female simultaneously or sequentially. The age at sexual maturity shows considerable intraspecific plasticity, with individuals raised on calcium-rich diets maturing several weeks earlier than those on calcium-poor substrates, underscoring the nutritional dependency of this life-history transition.

Once mature, Achatina achatina displays a maximum reproductive output that is characterized by the deposition of multiple clutches of eggs throughout the year. Females, acting in their capacity as egg layers following reciprocal copulation, produce a mean of 300 to 400 eggs per individual per year [Ri = 300 to 400 eggs per individual per year], with the highest recorded rates occurring continuously when ambient temperature is regulated at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This fecundity translates into a very high potential for population increase, as a single gravid adult can contribute hundreds of offspring annually to the next generation. The daily reproduction rate implicit in this annual figure reflects the species' capacity for nearly continuous oviposition during the warm, wet season. Each egg is roughly 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter, enclosed in a calcareous shell that provides physical protection and a reservoir of calcium for the developing embryo. The energetic cost of this sustained reproductive effort is considerable, and adults in peak laying condition exhibit significantly reduced somatic growth rates compared to immature conspecifics.

The asymptotic adult size of Achatina achatina is characterized by a maximum ultimate shell length of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters], a dimension that distinguishes it from many other giant african land snails. A representative individual of this species with a shell measuring 7.8 centimeters in length typically corresponds to a live wet weight of 59.2 grams , indicating a robust, heavy-bodied morphology consistent with a large-shelled detritivore. The relationship between shell length and wet weight is approximately isometric for most of the juvenile and sub-adult period, though weight gain accelerates during the final growth phase as the shell thickens and the visceral mass expands with the maturation of the albumen gland and reproductive organs. Final adult size is strongly influenced by the calcium availability in the substrate, with populations on limestone-derived soils achieving larger average dimensions than those on acidic, leached laterites. The shell itself displays the characteristic brown, orange-banded, or cream-colored spiral patterning typical of the species, serving both as a physical defense against predation and as a thermal buffer against midday insolation in its native West African forest floor habitat.
